title: How to Write a Resume That Gets Noticed by Hiring Managers
summary: Hiring managers often scan a resume in seconds. Learn how to structure yours so the most important points are seen first.
body:
A resume has one job: to earn you an interview. Hiring managers often review many applications for a single role, so yours needs to be clear, focused and easy to scan.

## Start with a strong summary

Open with two or three lines that describe who you are, what you do well, and the kind of role you want. Keep it specific to the job you are applying for.

## Show results, not just duties

Instead of listing what you were responsible for, describe what you achieved. Numbers help: how many people you served, how much time you saved, or how much a process improved.

## Keep it clean and honest

Use a simple layout, consistent fonts and clear headings. Keep it to one or two pages, proofread carefully, and never include anything you cannot back up in an interview.

title: 7 Common Interview Questions and How to Answer Them
summary: From “tell me about yourself” to “why should we hire you?”, here is how to prepare clear and confident answers.
body:
Most interviews follow a familiar pattern. If you prepare for the common questions, you will have more energy to handle the unexpected ones.

## Tell me about yourself

Give a short professional summary: where you are now, what you have done, and why you are excited about this role. Avoid retelling your whole life story.

## Why do you want this job?

Research the company before the interview. Mention something specific about its work, and connect it to your skills and goals.

## What are your strengths and weaknesses?

Choose strengths that match the role and support them with a short example. For weaknesses, be honest and explain what you are doing to improve.

Practise out loud with a friend or in front of a mirror. The goal is not to memorise answers, but to feel comfortable speaking about your experience.

title: Writing a Cover Letter That Stands Out
summary: A good cover letter connects your experience to the role. Here is a simple structure you can adapt for any application.
body:
Your cover letter is your chance to explain why you are a good fit in your own words. It should add to your resume, not repeat it.

## Address it properly

Whenever possible, address the letter to a named person. If the job post does not give a name, a professional greeting is fine.

## Keep to three short parts

Begin by stating the role you are applying for and why it interests you. Then share one or two examples of experience that match what the employer needs. Finish by thanking the reader and saying you would welcome a conversation.

Keep it to one page, and tailor each letter to the job. A generic letter is easy to spot.

title: How to Spot and Avoid Job Scams
summary: Genuine employers do not ask you to pay to get a job. Learn the warning signs that a vacancy may not be real.
body:
Unfortunately, job seekers are a common target for scammers. A few simple checks can protect your money and your personal information.

## Common warning signs

Be careful if you are asked to pay a fee for an interview, training, uniform or “registration”. Be wary of offers that seem too good to be true, vague job descriptions, and messages that pressure you to act immediately.

## Check before you apply

Look up the company and confirm that it exists. Check that the contact details match the company’s official website, and be cautious about free email addresses used for official hiring.

## Protect your information

Do not share bank details, passwords or copies of identity documents until you have confirmed that the employer is genuine and a formal offer has been made.

title: Building Your Professional Network From Scratch
summary: You do not need a big network to get started. Small, consistent steps can open doors to mentors and opportunities.
body:
Networking is simply building genuine relationships with people in your field. You do not have to be outgoing to do it well.

## Start with people you already know

Former classmates, colleagues, family friends and teachers can all be useful contacts. Let them know what kind of work you are looking for.

## Be useful, not just asking

Share helpful articles, congratulate people on their achievements, and offer help where you can. Relationships grow when they go both ways.

## Follow up

After meeting someone, send a short thank-you message. Staying in touch regularly is what turns a brief meeting into a lasting connection.

title: Following Up After You Apply: What to Say and When
summary: A polite follow-up shows interest and professionalism. Here is how to do it without being pushy.
body:
Waiting to hear back can be stressful. A short, polite follow-up can remind the employer of your application and show that you are serious about the role.

## When to follow up

If the job post gives a closing date or decision date, wait until it has passed. If not, a week or two after applying is a reasonable time to check in.

## What to include

Keep your message brief. Mention the role you applied for, restate your interest in one sentence, and ask whether there is any further information you can provide.

After an interview, send a thank-you message within a day or two. Whatever the outcome, stay polite and professional.
